games.title: Basics of Biosafety: quick quiz
games.blurb: Quiz for Year 2 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: Which of the following best defines biosafety in a clinical laboratory setting?
options: The practice of preventing contamination of the environment by pathogens
The use of personal protective equipment only
The disposal of all specimens in a standard trash bin
The sterilization of all instruments before use
questions.explanation: Biosafety encompasses measures to prevent release of pathogens into the environment.

questions.q: What is the primary purpose of a biosafety level (BSL) classification?
options: To determine the cost of laboratory equipment
To guide the design of laboratory ventilation systems
To specify the containment precautions required for a given organism
To dictate the number of staff allowed in a lab
questions.explanation: BSL levels dictate containment practices based on organism risk.

questions.q: Which of the following is a key component of BSL-3 containment?
options: Use of a biosafety cabinet type I
questions.explanation: Negative pressure ventilation is essential for BSL‑3 labs to prevent escape of aerosols.

questions.q: In epidemiology, the term "incidence" refers to:
options: The proportion of a population that has a disease at a specific time
The number of new cases occurring in a defined period
The total number of cases ever recorded
The severity of a disease outbreak
questions.explanation: Incidence measures new cases over a period.

questions.q: Which statistical measure is most appropriate for describing the central tendency of a normally distributed continuous variable?
questions.explanation: The mean best represents the center of a normal distribution.

questions.q: A 95% confidence interval for a proportion that is 0.30 with a margin of error of ±0.05 indicates that:
options: We are 95% confident the true proportion lies between 0.25 and 0.35
The interval is too wide to be useful
questions.explanation: The CI expresses where the true proportion likely falls.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a recommended practice for handling potentially infectious blood specimens?
options: Using a biosafety cabinet for all manipulations
Labeling specimens clearly with a biohazard symbol
Storing specimens at room temperature for extended periods
Using a closed system for transport
questions.explanation: Blood specimens should not be stored at room temperature for long periods.

questions.q: In a case‑control study, the odds ratio is used to estimate:
questions.explanation: The odds ratio approximates relative risk in case‑control designs.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes the term "pathogenicity"?
options: The ability of a microorganism to survive in the environment
The capacity of a microorganism to cause disease
The speed at which a disease spreads
The resistance of a pathogen to antibiotics
questions.explanation: Pathogenicity refers to disease-causing potential.

questions.q: The primary goal of a biosafety training program for laboratory personnel is to:
questions.explanation: Training ensures adherence to safety regulations and reduces risk.

games.title: Intestinal Stomas: Colostomy and Ileostomy, Types, Care and: quick quiz
games.topic: Intestinal Stomas: Colostomy and Ileostomy, Types, Care and
games.blurb: Quiz for Year 4 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: Which of the following is the most common indication for a permanent colostomy in the left colon?
options: A. Crohn's disease involving the terminal ileum
C. Colorectal cancer involving the sigmoid colon
D. Ischemic colitis of the ascending colon
questions.explanation: Colorectal cancer of the sigmoid colon is the most frequent pathology that ultimately requires a permanent colostomy in the left colon.

questions.q: A 45‑year‑old man with ulcerative colitis presents with toxic megacolon. Which surgical procedure is most appropriate?
options: D. Subtotal colectomy with ileorectal anastomosis
questions.explanation: Total colectomy with ileostomy is the definitive treatment for toxic megacolon, removing the diseased colon and preventing perforation.

questions.q: Which of the following is a contraindication to performing a loop ileostomy?
questions.explanation: Severe sepsis is a contraindication to creating a loop ileostomy because the patient’s systemic condition is too unstable for the procedure.

questions.q: What is the primary purpose of a diverting ileostomy in patients undergoing low anterior resection for rectal cancer?
options: C. To allow early enteral feeding
questions.explanation: A diverting ileostomy reduces the risk of anastomotic leak by diverting fecal stream away from the distal anastomosis.

questions.q: Which of the following is the most common complication of a colostomy?
questions.explanation: Peristomal hernia is the most frequent mechanical complication of colostomies, occurring when abdominal contents herniate through the stoma opening.

questions.q: A patient with an ileostomy has a daily output of 1.5 L. Which of the following is the first step in management?
questions.explanation: High‑output ileostomies are first managed by aggressive fluid and electrolyte replacement to prevent dehydration.

questions.q: Which of the following is a key component of stoma care education for patients?
options: A. How to perform a stoma reversal
B. How to identify stoma skin irritation
C. How to perform a colonoscopy
questions.explanation: Patients must learn to recognize and treat stoma skin irritation, which is a common issue that can lead to complications if not managed promptly.

questions.q: A loop colostomy is most often created in which part of the colon?
questions.explanation: Loop colostomies are usually placed in the sigmoid colon for diverting purposes, providing a convenient and low‑risk site.

questions.q: Which of the following is a contraindication to performing a permanent ileostomy?
questions.explanation: All listed conditions are contraindications to a permanent ileostomy because they indicate a patient who is not a suitable candidate for a long‑term stoma.

questions.q: What is the most appropriate timing for reversal of a loop ileostomy created for a low anterior resection?
questions.explanation: Reversal is typically performed 6–8 weeks after the initial surgery once the patient has recovered and the anastomosis is well healed.

games.title: Fluid and Electrolyte Disorders: case showdown
games.blurb: Case Showdown for Year 4 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: A 68‑year‑old man with a history of chronic kidney disease presents with confusion, lethargy, and a serum sodium of 128 mmol/L. He reports decreased oral intake and has a urine osmolality of 350 mOsm/kg. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Low serum sodium with relatively concentrated urine in a CKD patient suggests hypovolemic hyponatremia due to volume depletion.

questions.q: A 45‑year‑old woman with a history of type 2 diabetes presents with polyuria, polydipsia, and a serum potassium of 3.0 mmol/L. Her serum bicarbonate is 18 mmol/L. What is the next best step in management?
questions.explanation: Hyperglycemia drives osmotic diuresis and potassium loss; insulin will correct hyperglycemia and shift potassium intracellularly.

questions.q: A 22‑year‑old man is admitted for severe vomiting and abdominal pain. On examination, he has dry mucous membranes and a heart rate of 110 bpm. His serum sodium is 140 mmol/L and serum osmolality is 260 mOsm/kg. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Dehydration from vomiting causes hypovolemic hyponatremia with low serum osmolality.

questions.q: A 60‑year‑old woman with heart failure presents with worsening dyspnea. Her serum sodium is 132 mmol/L. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
questions.explanation: Loop diuretics reduce fluid overload and improve hyponatremia in heart failure.

questions.q: A 30‑year‑old man with a recent diagnosis of nephrotic syndrome has a serum sodium of 138 mmol/L and a serum osmolality of 280 mOsm/kg. He is euvolemic. What is the most likely cause of his hyponatremia?
questions.explanation: Nephrotic syndrome can cause SIADH leading to euvolemic hyponatremia.

questions.q: A 55‑year‑old woman presents with muscle cramps and a serum potassium of 2.8 mmol/L. She reports taking a thiazide diuretic for hypertension. What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.explanation: Adding a potassium‑sparing diuretic (e.g., spironolactone) helps prevent thiazide‑induced hypokalemia.

questions.q: A 70‑year‑old man with chronic liver disease presents with confusion and a serum sodium of 125 mmol/L. His serum osmolality is 270 mOsm/kg. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Hepatic encephalopathy with hyponatremia is often due to SIADH in cirrhosis.

questions.q: A 50‑year‑old woman with a history of chronic pancreatitis presents with abdominal pain and a serum bicarbonate of 12 mmol/L. Her serum sodium is 138 mmol/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Metabolic acidosis due to pancreatic insufficiency
questions.explanation: Pancreatic exocrine insufficiency can cause malabsorption and metabolic acidosis.

games.title: Paed 2021: case showdown
games.blurb: Case Showdown for Year 4 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: A 4‑year‑old boy presents with a 3‑day history of fever, sore throat, and a sudden, painless swelling of the left tonsil. Examination reveals a firm, non‑tender mass with a bluish hue and a normal cervical lymph node count. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A firm, non‑tender, bluish tonsillar mass in a child is classic for a tonsillar lymphoma (often a non‑Hodgkin lymphoma). Adenoid hypertrophy and tonsillar cysts are usually soft and may be tender, while a peritonsillar abscess is painful and often tender.

questions.q: A 2‑year‑old girl is brought in with a 2‑day history of cough, nasal congestion, and a high fever. On examination she has a red, bulging tympanic membrane and a low‑pitch, “whooping” cough. What is the next best step in management?
questions.explanation: The presentation is classic for pertussis. The first‑line treatment is a macrolide antibiotic, such as oral azithromycin (or erythromycin). Penicillin G is no longer recommended for pertussis.

questions.q: A 6‑month‑old infant presents with a sudden onset of vomiting, lethargy, and a high fever. He has a history of recent upper respiratory infection. Examination reveals a bulging fontanelle and a rapid, irregular heartbeat. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Bulging fontanelle, lethargy, and tachycardia in an infant are classic signs of meningitis. Sepsis can also present similarly, but the presence of a bulging fontanelle strongly points to meningitis.

questions.q: A 9‑year‑old boy has a 4‑week history of intermittent abdominal pain, weight loss, and occasional bloody stools. He also reports fatigue and a mild fever. Physical examination shows pallor and a tender, enlarged spleen. Which investigation should be performed first?
questions.explanation: The first step in evaluating a child with abdominal pain, weight loss, bloody stools, anemia, and splenomegaly is a complete blood count to assess for anemia, leukocytosis, and eosinophilia, which can guide further work‑up for inflammatory bowel disease or other causes.

questions.q: A 3‑year‑old girl presents with a sudden onset of high fever, rash, and a swollen, tender right knee. She has a history of a recent upper respiratory infection. Examination shows a red, hot knee with limited range of motion. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Acute, painful, swollen joint following a URI in a toddler is most consistent with septic arthritis, which requires urgent joint aspiration and antibiotics. Juvenile idiopathic arthritis is usually chronic, Lyme disease would have a characteristic rash, and gonococcal arthritis is rare in this age group.

questions.q: A 7‑year‑old boy is brought in with a 1‑day history of fever, sore throat, and a sudden, painless swelling of the left tonsil. Examination reveals a firm, non‑tender mass with a bluish hue and a normal cervical lymph node count. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The presentation is characteristic of a tonsillar lymphoma. Adenoid hypertrophy and tonsillar cysts are usually soft and may be tender, while a peritonsillar abscess is painful.

questions.q: A 5‑year‑old girl presents with a 2‑day history of fever, cough, and a sudden onset of a high‑pitch, “whooping” cough. Examination reveals a red, bulging tympanic membrane. What is the next best step in management?
questions.explanation: Pertussis is treated with a macrolide antibiotic such as oral azithromycin. Penicillin G is no longer the first‑line agent for pertussis.

questions.q: A 10‑month‑old infant presents with a sudden onset of vomiting, lethargy, and a high fever. He has a history of recent upper respiratory infection. Examination reveals a bulging fontanelle and a rapid, irregular heartbeat. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Bulging fontanelle, lethargy, and tachycardia are classic signs of meningitis in an infant.

games.title: Expert Immunohematology Assessment: drug duel
games.blurb: Drug Duel for Year 3 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: Which drug is most commonly used as a first‑line agent for the treatment of immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) in adults?
questions.explanation: Prednisone (or other corticosteroids) is the standard first‑line therapy for newly diagnosed adult ITP. IVIG is reserved for rapid platelet elevation or when steroids are contraindicated.

questions.q: What is the primary mechanism of action of eculizumab in the management of paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH)?
options: B. Blockade of the C5 complement protein
C. Induction of erythroid progenitor proliferation
questions.explanation: Eculizumab binds to complement protein C5, preventing its cleavage and the formation of the membrane attack complex, thereby reducing intravascular hemolysis.

questions.q: Which of the following drugs is a thrombopoietin receptor agonist used in refractory ITP?
questions.explanation: Romiplostim is a thrombopoietin receptor agonist that stimulates megakaryocyte proliferation and platelet production, used in refractory ITP.

questions.q: What is the characteristic side effect of rituximab that warrants pre‑medication with acetaminophen and antihistamine?
questions.explanation: Rituximab can cause infusion‑related hypersensitivity reactions; pre‑medication with acetaminophen and antihistamine helps prevent these events.

questions.q: Which drug is indicated for the treatment of severe aplastic anemia when a matched sibling donor is unavailable?
questions.explanation: Cyclosporine combined with antithymocyte globulin is the standard immunosuppressive regimen for severe aplastic anemia when a matched sibling donor is not available.

questions.q: Which agent is a complement inhibitor used in atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS)?
questions.explanation: Eculizumab blocks terminal complement activation (C5) and is indicated for aHUS.

questions.q: What is the main indication for the use of danazol in hematology?
options: A. Treatment of iron deficiency anemia
questions.explanation: Danazol has been used historically in refractory ITP and autoimmune hemolytic anemia, not for suppressing erythropoiesis in thalassemia.

questions.q: Which drug is a potent inhibitor of platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptors used in acute coronary syndromes?
questions.explanation: Eptifibatide is a reversible GP IIb/IIIa antagonist that prevents platelet aggregation in acute coronary syndromes.
